title: Air India Slashes Delhi Cargo Transfer Time to Five Hours as India Bids to Become Global Freight Hub
excerpt: A 90-day pilot on the Chennai-Delhi-Frankfurt corridor doubled daily cargo volumes and cut connection times by 85 percent, prompting expansion to five Indian cities and three European destinations.
body:
• Air India's cargo transshipment pilot reduced average connection time at Delhi Airport from 36–48 hours to just 5–8 hours by eliminating mandatory piece-level security re-screening.
  • Daily cargo volumes on the Chennai-Delhi-Frankfurt corridor doubled from 2.2 metric tonnes to 4.5 MT during the two-month proof of concept, with a 100 percent Flown-as-Booked rate and zero damage.
  • The expanded network now connects five Indian cities — Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad and Mumbai — to Copenhagen, Frankfurt and London Heathrow.
  • Delhi alone could potentially attract more than two million metric tonnes of additional annual transshipment cargo across 95+ international corridors, challenging established hubs like Dubai and Singapore.

A Policy Fix That Removed a 24-Hour Bottleneck

Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu inaugurated the expanded phase of India's cargo transshipment reform at Delhi Airport's Transshipment Excellence Centre on August 19, marking the formal scaling up of a pilot that has quietly transformed how air freight moves through the country.

The problem it solved was straightforward but costly. Under the old system, a consignment flying from Chennai to Frankfurt via Delhi had to be unpacked at Delhi Airport. Every individual package underwent mandatory security re-screening before the shipment was rebuilt and loaded onto its onward flight. That process alone could add more than 24 hours to transit times, according to Air India, while increasing the risk of damage and pilferage.

The new framework, approved by the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS), allows eligible cargo to remain securely packed within the same Unit Load Device throughout its journey. No unpacking, no piece-level re-screening — just prescribed security controls at the container level.

"This reformed cargo transshipment policy has the potential to be a game-changer for India's air cargo sector. By enabling seamless cargo transfers through Delhi, it can help attract transit traffic that currently moves through foreign gateways."

— Ramesh Mamidala, Head of Cargo, Air India

The Numbers Behind the Pilot

Air India launched the 90-day proof of concept on the Chennai-Delhi-Frankfurt sector on June 20, 2026. The results over the first two months were striking. Average cargo connection time at Delhi fell from 36–48 hours to 5–8 hours — an 85 percent reduction. Daily volumes on the corridor doubled from 2.2 metric tonnes to 4.5 MT.

Between June 20 and August 20, the airline transported 300 metric tonnes of cargo on the route. Flown-as-Booked performance climbed from 76 percent to a perfect 100 percent, with zero cargo loss or damage recorded during the entire period. Top-tier freight forwarders including DHL, Dachser, DVS and Kuehne+Nagel reported highly positive feedback, according to the airline.

The government has now approved expansion to four additional domestic origin stations — Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Mumbai — alongside Chennai, connecting to three European destinations: Copenhagen, Frankfurt and London Heathrow. The expanded network is expected to increase Air India's monthly cargo volumes on these routes from 1,763 tonnes to 3,183 tonnes, representing nearly 80 percent growth.

India's Bid to Challenge Global Transit Hubs

The reform fits into a broader government strategy to position India as a global cargo transshipment hub. Currently, much of the air freight moving between South Asia and Europe or the Americas routes through established hubs in the Gulf states and Southeast Asia. India's geographic position between East and West offers a natural advantage, but cumbersome regulations have historically made its airports less competitive for transit cargo.

The scale of the opportunity is significant. Air India estimates that Delhi alone could attract more than two million metric tonnes of additional annual transshipment cargo across more than 95 international corridors. The benefits would extend beyond airlines to freight forwarders, e-commerce companies, warehousing providers, ground handlers and other logistics businesses.

"We are now scaling up this successful model by connecting four more major domestic cargo markets and two new international destinations. Our larger ambition is to position India as a global cargo transshipment hub by leveraging our strategic location between the East and the West."

— Ram Mohan Naidu, Union Minister for Civil Aviation

What Comes Next

Subject to regulatory approvals, the transshipment framework will be progressively extended across all domestic-to-international cargo movements, including narrowbody bulk cargo operations. The government also plans to enable international-to-domestic and international-to-international cargo transshipment through Indian airports — the latter being the segment where Gulf hubs currently dominate.

For Indian businesses and the diaspora, faster cargo movement through Delhi translates directly into shorter delivery times for shipments between India and Europe. E-commerce orders, personal shipments and business freight that currently face multi-day delays at transit points could move significantly faster as the framework scales up. The proof of concept's flawless damage record also addresses a persistent concern about the integrity of goods transiting through Indian airports.

The phased rollout will test whether India can convert a successful pilot into a systemic advantage. If it does, Delhi's emergence as a competitive international cargo hub would mark a significant shift in global air freight routing — one driven not by new infrastructure but by a regulatory reform that simply eliminated an unnecessary bottleneck.
